# Preface {-}

```{r fig.align='center', out.height="300px", echo=FALSE, include=identical(knitr:::pandoc_to(), 'html')}
knitr::include_graphics('img/cover.png', dpi = NA)
```

In applied econometric research and business analytics alike, many steps in handling digital data are involved before running regression estimations and training machine learning algorithms. While often neglected in statistics and econometrics curricula, the steps of gathering, cleaning, storing, and filtering data for research/analytics purposes are of utmost importance to ensure accurate and reproducible analytic insights. This book first introduces foundational concepts about data and data processing, and then guides the reader through each step of how to get from the raw data to the final data analysis output.

## Who This Book Is For {.unnumbered}

This book is designed for:

- **Undergraduate students** in economics, business, political science, sociology, and other quantitative social sciences who need practical data skills for coursework and research
- **Graduate students** beginning empirical research who need to bridge the gap between theoretical statistics and practical data work
- **Practitioners** working with data in analytics, policy analysis, or research roles who lack a formal computer science background

The book assumes basic familiarity with undergraduate statistics (means, standard deviations, correlation, and the general idea of regression) and some exposure to economics or social science research questions. No prior programming experience is required—we start from the fundamentals.

## Why R? {.unnumbered}

This book uses R as its primary tool. R was designed specifically for statistical computing and has become the dominant language in academic economics and social science research. The `tidyverse` ecosystem provides an intuitive and consistent approach to data manipulation, and `ggplot2` is widely regarded as one of the best tools for statistical visualization.

That said, Python is an excellent alternative—particularly if you plan to work in machine learning or production software environments. The concepts in this book (data structures, cleaning, reshaping, joining) transfer directly to Python's `pandas` library. Chapter 2 discusses this choice in more detail.

## How to Use This Book {.unnumbered}

The book is organized into three parts:

- **Part I (Foundations)** covers programming basics, how computers store and process data, and the fundamental data structures you'll work with in R
- **Part II (Data Types)** explores specialized data formats: hierarchical data (JSON, XML), text data, and image data
- **Part III (The Data Pipeline)** walks through the practical workflow: importing data, cleaning and transforming it, exploring patterns, basic statistical modeling, and visualization

Each chapter includes worked examples with real data, and tutorials that integrate multiple concepts. Key takeaways at the end of each chapter summarize the main points.

You can read the book front-to-back, or use it as a reference—jumping to specific chapters as needed for your current project.

## Prerequisites {.unnumbered}

To follow along with the examples, you will need:

- R (version 4.0 or later recommended): https://cran.r-project.org/
- RStudio (or another IDE): https://posit.co/download/rstudio-desktop/
- The `tidyverse` package collection: `install.packages("tidyverse")`

Additional packages are introduced as needed throughout the book.

## Package Versions {.unnumbered}

This book was developed and tested with R version `r getRversion()` and the following core package versions:

```{r package-versions, echo=FALSE, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
pkgs <- c("tidyverse", "ggplot2", "dplyr", "tidyr", "readr",
          "stringr", "quanteda", "jsonlite", "xml2", "rvest")
installed <- sapply(pkgs, function(p) {
    v <- tryCatch(as.character(packageVersion(p)), error = function(e) "not installed")
    v
})
pkg_df <- data.frame(Package = pkgs, Version = installed)
knitr::kable(pkg_df, col.names = c("Package", "Version"))
```

Package versions can affect reproducibility—functions may be renamed, arguments changed, or behaviors modified between versions. If you encounter unexpected errors or different results, check whether your package versions match those listed above. You can check your installed version with `packageVersion("packagename")` and install a specific version using `remotes::install_version("packagename", version = "x.y.z")` if needed. See Chapter 2 for more on package management and reproducibility.

## Exercises {.unnumbered}

Each chapter ends with exercises designed to reinforce the material. These range from conceptual questions to hands-on coding problems. Working through them is the best way to solidify your understanding. Selected solutions are provided in Appendix C—but try the exercises yourself before checking!

## Conventions Used in This Book {.unnumbered}

Throughout this book, you will encounter several types of highlighted boxes designed to enhance your learning:

> **In Practice:** These boxes connect concepts to real-world applications. They describe how researchers, analysts, and practitioners actually use the techniques in academic research, business analytics, and policy work—often citing relevant literature and providing concrete examples.

> **Common Error:** These boxes highlight frequent mistakes and misconceptions. Learning what *not* to do is just as important as learning correct approaches. Pay special attention to these—they address pitfalls that trip up many beginners.

> **AI Support Prompt:** These boxes provide prompts you can use with AI assistants like ChatGPT or Claude to deepen your understanding, get additional practice exercises, debug your code, or receive personalized explanations. AI tools excel at providing interactive feedback and can help you work through challenging concepts at your own pace. The prompts are designed as templates—fill in the bracketed placeholders with your own data, code, or questions.

Each chapter concludes with a **Key Takeaways** section that summarizes the most important concepts and skills covered. These summaries are useful for review and for quickly recalling material when you return to the book as a reference.

Code examples appear in monospace font with syntax highlighting. Output from R is shown with `##` prefixes. When you see code blocks, we encourage you to type them into R yourself rather than copying and pasting—the muscle memory helps with learning.
